Passage (no passage) Question The result of increasing the quantity \(x\) by \(400\%\) is \(60\). What is the value of \(x\)?
rationale: Step 1: Write the multiplier before doing anything else. Increasing a quantity by \(p\%\) multiplies it by \(\left(1 + \frac{p}{100}\right)\) — the original amount is still there, and the increase is added on top. For \(p = 400\): \(1 + \frac{400}{100} = 1 + 4 = 5\). So "increased by 400%" means ×5 , not ×4. Step 2: Solve. \(5x = 60 \;\Rightarrow\; x = 12\). Step 3: Check. \(12 \times 5 = 60\). Confirm it reads correctly as a percent increase: the increase itself is \(60 - 12 = 48\), and \(\frac{48}{12} = 4 = 400\%\). The increase is 400% of the original , exactly as stated. Why the distractors fail: B. 15 — the choice actually selected, and the whole point of the question. It comes from reading "400%" as the multiplier itself: \(4x = 60 \Rightarrow x = 15\). But ×4 is what "increased by 300 %" means, since \(1 + 3 = 4\). Checking would have caught it: \(15 \to 60\) is an increase of \(45\), and \(\frac{45}{15} = 3 = 300\%\). C. 20 — treating the phrase as "increased to 300%" or otherwise dividing by 3. Neither matches the wording. D. 240 — multiplying instead of dividing (\(60 \times 4\)), i.e. running the operation in the wrong direction. \(60\) is already the result , so \(x\) must be smaller than \(60\); any answer above \(60\) is eliminable on sight. Takeaway rule: never let a percent go straight into the equation. Write the multiplier on paper first — increase by \(p\%\) → \(\times\left(1 + \frac{p}{100}\right)\) , decrease by \(p\%\) → \(\times\left(1 - \frac{p}{100}\right)\) — then substitute. Percentages above 100 are where this leaks: +100% is ×2, +200% is ×3, +400% is ×5. Explanation written by Claude. Math · Hard · Problem Solving & Data Analysis · Percentages Trap you fell for: B. Read 400% as the multiplier (×4) instead of the increase (×5).

That is a complete sentence — subject sculptures , verb are made — with "Creations so small…" as an opening modifier. Everything before the blank, "Jamaican British artist Willard Wigan is known for his remarkable microsculptures," is also complete. Step 2: Independent + independent means a hard stop. The giveaway is that the material after the blank does not stop at the appositive — it runs on into a second subject and verb ("Wigan's sculptures are made"), which an appositive cannot do. D. microsculptures and creations — and joins the two nouns into a compound object of for , which leaves "Wigan's sculptures are made from…" with no connection to the front of the sentence. Takeaway rule: before choosing punctuation, read from the blank to the end of the sentence and ask "can this stand alone?" Which function V gives the volume of the prism, in cubic inches, in terms of the length of the base?
rationale: Step 1 — Translate the comparison. 'The length (x) is 7 more than the width (w).' Write it as an equation: x = w + 7. Solving for w: w = x − 7. Step 2 — Write the volume formula. Volume of a rectangular prism = length × width × height = x · (x − 7) · 9 = 9x(x − 7). So V(x) = 9x(x − 7). Step 3 — Why C fails. C uses x + 7, which would mean the width is x + 7. But 'x is 7 MORE THAN the width' means x is the larger quantity, so width = x − 7, not x + 7. Choosing + 7 reverses the comparison direction — the same direction-of-comparison flip logged in the PT6 variable-order loss. Step 4 — Confirm D. V(x) = 9x(x − 7): height 9, length x, width x − 7. Plug in a test: if x = 10, then width = 3. Volume = 9 · 10 · 3 = 270. Check: length (10) is 7 more than width (3) ✓. V(10) = 9·10·3 = 270 ✓. Rule: Always translate 'A is N more than B' as an equation (A = B + N → B = A − N) before substituting. Never read the comparison direction from the English directly into a formula without the intermediate step. Explanation written by Claude. Math · Hard · Advanced Math · Nonlinear functions

No punctuation between two independent clauses is a fused/run-on sentence. Step 7 — Why D is correct. Left side (independent clause) + colon + right side (explanation of 'indiscriminate'). The colon signals 'here is what I mean by that word.' ✓ Pattern note: When the right clause explains a specific word in the left clause, a colon is almost always correct. Passage While recent scholarship has undermined claims that the works of the twelfth-century Andalusian philosopher Ibn Rushd (Averroes) were ______ other Muslim philosophers of his time, it is indisputable that his geographic location meant his works were primarily available through Latin translations in Europe rather than in the Islamic world. Question Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
rationale: Step 1 — Parse the sentence structure. 'Scholarship has UNDERMINED CLAIMS THAT his works were [blank] other Muslim philosophers.' This is a double negative: scholarship undermines the claim. So the blank holds the OLD CLAIM, which is now being disproved. Step 2 — What does the rest of the sentence tell us? 'His works were primarily available through Latin translations in Europe rather than in the Islamic world.' This implies his works did not circulate widely among Muslim philosophers — his influence on that group was limited/minimal. Step 3 — What was the claim being undermined? The claim that his works were [blank] other Muslim philosophers. The second half tells us his works weren't available to them → so the OLD CLAIM must have been that he DID have some impact on them. But the double-negative says: scholarship now undermines the claim that he mattered to them. So the blank = 'consequential/influential' or at minimum NOT 'inconsequential.' Wait — actually, reversed: the claim being undermined is that he WAS inconsequential to them. Scholarship shows he actually WAS consequential. OR: scholarship undermines the claim that he WAS consequential. The second-half evidence (works only reached via Latin) supports 'inconsequential.' Re-read: scholarship undermines claims that his works were [blank] to/among other Muslim philosophers. If blank = 'inconsequential to,' then the claim being undermined is 'his works were inconsequential to Muslim philosophers.' Since scholarship undermines this claim, scholarship shows he WAS consequential. But the second half says his works circulated mainly in Europe — contradicting consequential impact in the Islamic world. The correct reading: scholarship undermines the claim he was inconsequential → he WAS impactful. But his works reached Europe, not the Islamic world. This is consistent: his European influence was great; the claim that he was inconsequential (to Muslim philosophy broadly) is what's being revised. Why C fails: 'imitated by' means Muslim philosophers copied his work. The sentence structure shows this claim is being undermined (shown false). But there's no logical reason the second clause (about Latin translations in Europe) specifically undermines 'imitated by.' D fits the logic better. Why D is correct: 'inconsequential to other Muslim philosophers' was the old claim (now undermined by scholarship showing he was actually consequential). His works reached them mainly via Europe, but scholars now recognize his influence on the broader tradition. D passes the logical-structure test. ✓ Key technique: bracket 'scholarship has undermined claims that' and focus on what the second clause implies about the blank. Then test each choice. Explanation written by Claude. Reading & Writing · Hard · Information and Ideas · Words in Context

options: Traceable to the Mount Sinai Monastery, one circa 550 CE icon features Saint Theodore, Saint George, and two angels among the individuals that it depicts.
The two angels positioned at the center of the Mount Sinai icon look away from the viewer, while the saints towards the sides of the icon look directly at the viewer.

answer: ["B \u2014 The two angels positioned at the center of the Mount Sinai icon look away from the viewer, while the saints towards the sides of the icon look directly at the viewer."]
rationale: Step 1 — Identify the goal: The student wants to describe a contrast within the Mount Sinai icon — how different figures are depicted based on their status. The correct choice must set the angels against the saints on both dimensions the notes track: gaze (toward vs. away) and position (center vs. side). Remaining steps written by Claude (OnePrep's were locked). Eliminate A: It merely lists who the icon depicts (Theodore, George, two angels). No contrast — no comparison of gaze or position. Off goal. Eliminate C: It states a general principle plus one fact (angels look away). It describes only the angels, not the saints, so there is no contrast. Half the comparison is missing. Eliminate D: It gets the details backwards/incomplete — it says the saints look outward (true) and the angels are toward the center (true) but omits the angels' gaze away , and more importantly it doesn't frame the two facts as opposed. It reads as a list, not a contrast, and drops the angels' averted gaze that is the sharpest point of difference. Confirm B: It explicitly pits the two groups against each other — angels at the center look away , saints at the sides look directly at the viewer. Both the gaze axis and the position axis are contrasted in one sentence, exactly matching the notes. Only B delivers the contrast. rationale: Step 1: Identify the two clauses. The sentence consists of two distinct ideas: the goal of National Buy Nothing Day and the debate regarding its actual effectiveness. These are two independent clauses that could stand as separate sentences. Remaining steps written by Claude (OnePrep's were locked). Step 2: Decide what job "though" is doing. "Though" can work two ways: as a subordinating conjunction ("though X is true, Y") or as a parenthetical adverb ("Y, though, is true"). Here it sits at the front of the second clause, so it must be read as a subordinating conjunction — it converts "the efficacy of such restraint... is open to dispute" into a dependent clause. A dependent clause can be joined to the preceding independent clause with a single comma. Correctly punctuated: "…refrain from new purchases for 24 hours, though the efficacy of such restraint—particularly over the long term—is open to dispute." Step 3: Rule out each wrong choice. C. hours, — with "though" removed, you have two full independent clauses joined by only a comma. That is a comma splice. A. hours, though; — the semicolon must separate two independent clauses. Placing it after "though" strands "though" at the end of the first clause (where it reads as a trailing adverb) and then requires the second clause to stand alone, producing a garbled boundary. You cannot follow a subordinating conjunction with a semicolon. D. hours, though, — the pair of commas turns "though" into a parenthetical aside, which means it no longer subordinates the second clause. Strip the aside and you are back to two independent clauses joined by a comma — a comma splice again. B. hours, though — one comma, "though" attached to the clause it subordinates. Correct. Takeaway rule: for Boundaries items, first mark each side of the blank as independent (I) or dependent (D). I + I needs a period, semicolon, or comma + FANBOYS. I + D takes just a comma. Then check whether the connector word is inside the second clause (subordinator) or fenced off by commas (parenthetical) — that single distinction decides A/B/D here. The radius of the circle is \(9\), and the distance from the center \(O\) to the external point \(P\) is \(15\). What is the length of \(\overline{PT}\)?
rationale: Step 1: Use the tangent–radius property. A tangent line is perpendicular to the radius drawn to the point of tangency. So angle \(OTP\) is a right angle, and triangle \(OTP\) is a right triangle with the right angle at \(T\) — not at \(O\) and not at \(P\). Step 2: Identify the hypotenuse correctly. The hypotenuse is always opposite the right angle, so it is \(\overline{OP}\), the center-to-external-point distance of \(15\). The radius \(9\) and the tangent \(PT\) are the two legs. Step 3: Solve. \(PT = \sqrt{OP^2 - OT^2} = \sqrt{15^2 - 9^2} = \sqrt{225 - 81} = \sqrt{144} = 12\). Why the distractors fail: C. \(\sqrt{306}\) — the single most common error: treating \(15\) as a leg and adding (\(\sqrt{15^2+9^2}\)). This happens when the right angle is placed at \(O\) instead of at \(T\). If \(15\) is the distance to the center , it must be the longest side. A. 6 — subtracting the lengths directly (\(15 - 9\)) instead of using the Pythagorean theorem. This is the distance from \(P\) to the near edge of the circle along line \(OP\), a different segment entirely. D. 24 — adding the lengths (\(15 + 9\)), the distance from \(P\) to the far edge of the circle along line \(OP\). Also not the tangent. Takeaway rule: on any circle-plus-external-point problem, draw the radius to the point of tangency first. That radius is perpendicular to the tangent, which fixes the hypotenuse as the center-to-point distance. Then \(\text{tangent} = \sqrt{d^2 - r^2}\). Explanation written by Claude. A circle with center \(O\) and radius \(9\). An external point \(P\) lies \(15\) units from \(O\). Segment \(PT\) is drawn from \(P\) so that it touches the circle at exactly one point, \(T\) (the point of tangency). Radius \(OT\) is drawn to that point, forming triangle \(OTP\) with \(OT = 9\) and \(OP = 15\). For the sentence to be complete, we need a main (finite) verb to follow this subject. Remaining steps written by Claude (OnePrep's were locked). Step 2: See why the sentence currently has no verb. Strip the relative clause "that are themselves organic" (its verb are belongs to that , not to Materials ). What remains is "Materials _ in next-generation solar panels…" — the blank is the only slot left for the sentence's main verb. So the answer must be a finite verb phrase , not an infinitive or a bare participle. Step 3: Rule out each wrong choice. A. to be incorporated — an infinitive. Infinitives are non-finite and cannot serve as a main verb, leaving the sentence a fragment: "Materials… to be incorporated in solar panels." Standing alone after the subject it can be read as a past participle continuing the modifier chain ("Materials that are themselves organic, incorporated in…"), which again yields a fragment. Even read as a simple past tense, it wrongly asserts that this has already been done, whereas the passage frames it as a discovered possibility demonstrated by a prototype greenhouse.
